div.p: We provide a constant time schedulability test and priority assignment algorithm for an on-line multiprocessor server handling aperiodic tasks. Dhall´s effect is avoided by dividing tasks in two priority classes based on their utilization: heavy and light. The improvement in this paper is due to assigning priority of light tasks based on slack -not on deadlines. We prove that if the load on the multi-

, the server can accept an incoming aperiodic task and guarantee that the deadlines of all accepted tasks will be met. This is better than the current state-ofthe-art algorithm where the priorities of light tasks are based on deadlines (the corresponding bound is in that case 35.425%).

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Many embedded real-time services are implemented as multiprocessors that handle a number of incoming aperiodic requests (tasks). One would like to guarantee certain response times for such tasks in high performance real-time services. The way to do this is to reject tasks that may not be able to meet their response times or could jeopardize the response time of other tasks. Previous results by Abdelzhar and Lu [1] make this possible by providing a schedulability test that can be used in admission control in uni-processor servers (these results were later extended to tasks that share resources [3]). The priority assigned to each aperiodic task is time independent, meaning that a certain task, with a certain relative deadline, will get the same priority independently when it arrives to the system. This result was later generalized to global (non-partitioned) multiprocessor scheduling by Abdelzhar et al. [2] for a limited type of tasks called liquid tasks, and then to general task patterns by Lundberg and Lennerstad [9].

Previous results on global multiprocessor realtime scheduling show that one cannot use the rate deadline monotonic priority assignment scheme since this may lead to missed deadlines even if the multiprocessor utilization is very low. The reason for this is the so-called Dhall´s effect [7]. The stateof-the-art technique for doing priority assignment in such cases was initially developed by Andersson et al [4], and then later improved by Lundberg [9] [10]. Based on the task utilizations, tasks are grouped into two categories: light tasks and heavy tasks. The heavy tasks get the highest priority, and in the original version the light tasks are assigned priority based on deadlines.

This priority assignment algorithm is in this paper improved by assigning task priorities to light tasks based on slack and not on deadline. It is well known that priority assignment based on deadlines is optimal for uni-processors, but in this paper we show that the worst-case behavior of slack-based priorities is better when there are three or more processors. This means that for three processors or more the priority assignment algorithm presented in this paper can schedule more task sets, i.e. task sets with a lower synthetic utilization (to be defined later), compared to the previous state of the art priority assignment algorithms for global multiprocessor scheduling of aperiodic tasks.

div.head: Problem Definition and Results
div.p: Independent aperiodic tasks arrive at a multiprocessor-based real-time system at random without prior knowledge from the scheduler. The multiprocessor schedules the arrived tasks by arranging them in a single queue and dequeues them in priority order when a processor becomes available. We assume preemptive scheduling. A preempted task is put back into the queue, and can later be restarted on any processor in the system. There is no overhead for switching from one task to another. We assume m identical processors.

A task T i constitutes a single invocation, defined by an arrival time A i , a worst-case execution time C i , and a relative deadline D i . The absolute deadline of the task is A i + D i . We define the utilization U i and slack S i for T i such that
div.formula: U i = C i /D i and S i = D i -C i .
div.p: To compute the utilization of an aperiodic workload, we use a concept called synthetic utilization. Defined in the following way: Let V(t) be the set of tasks for which
div.formula: A i t < A i + D i . The synthetic utili- zation is then US(t) = ) (t V i T i U /m. The maximal synthetic utilization is US max = max t US(t).
div.p: For periodic tasks one has traditionally classified a scheduling policy as either fixed priority or dynamic priority, where each invocation of a periodic task will have the same priority when using a fixed priority scheme. This classification is inappropriate for aperiodic tasks. Scheduling policies for aperiodic task can instead be classified as either timeindependent or time-dependent [1]. A scheduling policy is time-independent if the priority assigned to a task does not depend on its arrival time. In our case, this means that the priority of task T i should be calculated from C i and D i .

Due to the so called Dhall's effect, the deadline monotonic priority assignment algorithm, which is optimal for the uni-processor case, is not optimal for global multiprocessor scheduling. Assigning priority based on the slack S i (least slack priority assignment: T j has higher priority than T i , iff S j < S i ) suffers from similar problems (also referred to as Dhall's effect in this paper, see Figure 1), i.e. such priority assignment can result in missed deadlines even if the synthetic utilization is very low. The problem is that a task with high utilization may miss its deadline due to interference from a number of tasks with low utilizations even if the (total) synthetic utilization is very low. It turns out that Dhall's effect is not quite as problematic for slack-based priority assignment as for the traditional deadlinebased approach. This is the reason why the algorithm described in this paper is better than the previous approaches (which are based on deadline monotone priority assignment).
For uni-processor systems and aperiodic tasks, Abdelzaher and Lu [1]

is an optimal utilization bound, independent on the number of processors.
Lundberg and Lennerstad generalized this result to any set of aperiodic tasks -not only liquid tasks [9].
In that case the corresponding bound is %.

Previous results [4][9] [10] show that the problems with Dhall's effect can be handled by dividing the tasks into two categories based on their utilization U i . Tasks for which U i > U threshold (m) are heavy tasks, and are assigned the highest priority in the system, The priority among the heavy tasks are determined by their utilization; the higher the utilization the higher priority. Tasks for which U i U threshold (m) are light tasks. For light tasks the highest priority has in the previous studies been assigned to the task with lowest D i , which is called deadline monotonic priority assignment. In this priority assignment the priority of each light task is less than the priority of any heavy task.

Here we use the same strategy with the modification that the priorities of light tasks are based on slack and not on deadlines. With this strategy the highest priority among light tasks is assigned to the task with lowest slack S i . We call the strategy the least slack priority assignment. For m < 3, priorities of light tasks based on deadlines is better [9]. For m 3 it is better to assign priorities to light tasks based on slack, and for this case we calculate a formula for the optimal utilization threshold U threshold (m): We show that all task patterns for which the synthetic utilization is always lower than or equal to U threshold (m) can be scheduled on m processors. We also show that this threshold is the best possible for this assignment strategy.

div.head: Definitions, Notations and Overview
div.p: We consider a multiprocessor receiving arbitrary aperiodic tasks. Among the set of all task patterns, some are schedulable, and some are not. Our aim is to calculate a bound U bound (m) so that all task patterns with US max U bound (m) are schedulable. Here we calculate the smallest such bound possible within the problem formulation. Associated with this bound is a value U threshold (m) such that tasks with an individual utilization smaller than or equal to U threshold (m) are categorized as light and tasks with an individual utilization larger than U threshold (m) are categorized as heavy. It turns out that U bound (m) = U threshold (m), and we will in the remaining text only use the notation U threshold (m) for both these roles.

Let a critically schedulable task pattern be a schedulable task pattern with some task T n such that if the execution time C n would be increased with an arbitrary small amount, T n would miss its deadline.

Within the set of such patterns, the worst-case critically schedulable task patterns are the task patterns where US max is minimal. We remark that there is no critically schedulable task pattern with US max < U threshold (m) by the definition of U threshold (m).

We start by considering all tasks as light, i.e. we assume that U threshold (m) is larger than the utilization of each task. We will show that the minimal US max for which a task pattern may miss a deadline is a decreasing function of U threshold (m), since Dhall's effect becomes more problematic when there is at least one task T i with high U i among the light tasks (see Figure 1). Consequently, in order to obtain our results, we first compute the synthetic utilization for worst-case critically schedulable task patterns with a given utilization U n of T n . This synthetic utilization is denoted u m (x) -it depends on the number of processors m. It is a function of x = U n = C n /D n . We will show that u m (x) is a decreasing function of x, and hence the worst-case scenario occurs when x = U n = U threshold (m), i.e. T n is as heavy as possible while still being a light task.

We also show that any task pattern with U thresh- old (m) < US max may miss a deadline if all tasks (except T n ) are considered as heavy. This leads to the equation x x u m ) ( . The optimal U threshold (m) is the solution to this equation, i.e. U threshold (m) = x for the x that solves the equation.

Since a task can only be blocked by tasks with higher priority, there is a worst-case critically schedulable task pattern such that T n is the task with the lowest priority and hence the longest S i in the pattern (we are considering only light tasks at the moment).

By the response time of a task we mean the time from the arrival of the task to the time when the task has completed all its execution. The response time must be lower than or equal to the deadline of the task.
A task T 1 interferes with task T 2 if removal of task T 1 lowers the response time of task T 2 .

A set of tasks T i (i < n) which all have higher priority than T n causes block interference on T n if all tasks in the set interferes with T n and furthermore the following holds: If we temporary remove T n from the task pattern, then for each time t (A n t A n + D n ) all m processors are either busy executing tasks or all processors are idle. I.e., they have equal size or behave as having so (some may consist of several smaller tasks).

If we assume that the time unit is the processor clock cycle (or whatever the smallest time unit can be on the computer system), then there are mD n clock cycles in the interval A n to A n + D n since there are m processors. If we temporary remove T n from the task pattern, then some of these cycles are busy executing tasks and the others are idle. We refer to the number of busy cycles as the demand in the interval A n to A n + D n .

div.head: Characterizing Critical Task Patterns
div.p: Here we characterize a critically schedulable task pattern that we may parameterize by one variable x = U n . With this task pattern a sharp bound can be calculated. In this section we assume that all tasks are light.

If we temporary remove task T n from a critically schedulable task pattern, and look at the period A n to A n + D n , then there must be exactly D n -C n time units when all processors are busy (follows from the definition of critically schedulable task patterns).

We can clearly remove all tasks that start after A n + D n , and still have a critically schedulable task pattern. If some task T i (in a critically schedulable task pattern) executes x i time units after A n + D n we can replace that task with a task T i ´such that A i ' = A i , C i ' = C i -x i , and D i ' = D i -x i . Note that S i ' = S i and U i ' < U i , and we still have a critically schedulable task pattern. This means that we only need to consider critically schedulable task patterns that contain task with a deadline smaller than

div.p: In the rest of this paper we will only consider such task patterns.
If we assume that the demand in the interval A n to A n + D n is constant, then Lemma 1 tells us that block interference is the worst-case scenario.

Lemma 1: Consider a task T x with the lowest priority in the interval A x to A x + D x . If the demand in the time interval A x to A x + D x is constant, then the re-sponse time for T x is maximized if we have block interference on T x .

Proof: The response time of T x is C x plus the time T x is blocked waiting for high priority tasks. T x is blocked waiting for high priority tasks when all m processors are busy. From its definition it is clear that for a constant number of busy clock cycles generated by other tasks than T x (i.e. for a constant demand) the time when all processors are busy is maximized by block interference.

div.p: We now only consider worst-case critically schedulable task patterns such that no task T i has an arrival time A i < A n , (see Theorem 1). We also introduce the parameter x = U n , and the strategy of dividing tasks in light and heavy.

Let US' = US max -U n /m. Lemma 2 tells us that for US' = y we can generate block interference on T n during at most y(2D n -C n ) clock cycles. The task pattern described in the proof of Lemma 3 ensures that this kind of block interference can be obtained. Without loss of generality we assume that D n = 1 and C n = x, making U n = x and S n = 1 -x. Since we are looking for a worst-case critically schedulable task pattern we know that y(2D n -C n ) = S n , which means that y(2x) = 1 -x. This means that the minimum utilization US' that we need to create a critically schedulable task pattern is a function of x (U n ), i.e. g(x) = (1 -x)/(2x). If we also consider the contribution to the synthetic utilization from T n itself, we need to add U n /m = x/m. Hence, the minimum US max is given by the formula f m (x) = (1 -x)/(2 -x) + x/m, where x = U n , if all tasks are considered as light.

Note that f m (1) = 1/m, i.e. almost zero for large m. The reason for this is Dhall's effect, which is a problem if all tasks are light. However, when we have m heavy tasks we cannot accept any other tasks without resorting to a time consuming analysis. div.head: Conclusions
div.p: We have improved the state-of-the-art priority assignment technique for aperiodic tasks [10]. Based on the utilization of each task, the priority assignment algorithm groups tasks into two categories: light tasks and heavy tasks. A task is heavy if its utilization is above a certain threshold, otherwise the task is light. The priorities of light have up to now been based on their deadlines.

The main contribution in this paper is that we have replaced the traditional priority assignment strategy for light tasks from shortest deadline to least slack first. It turns out that the worst-case behavior of the slackbased approach is better when there are three or more processors. The practical implication of the results presented here is that we are able to schedule more task patterns with guaranteed deadlines using the slack-based approach presented here compared to the traditional deadline-based approach.
We also provide an optimal threshold value , where m > 2.

This is a decreasing function in m. Hence, m gives a bound valid but not optimal for all multiprocessors. We obtain The quantity U threshold (m) plays two roles. It is a threshold for the synthetic utilization in the admission control of incoming tasks, and it is a threshold for the categorization of light and heavy tasks. We have provided an optimal threshold and improved the state-ofthe-art priority assignment algorithm for aperiodic tasks. As a consequence of this, for m > 2 we provide the best fixed time admission control test known to us; the test is best in the sense that we are accepting a maximum number of tasks while still guaranteeing that all deadlines will be met.
